title: SUCCESS CHANGED HIM.
paragraphs: SUCCESS CHANGED HIM.

He started humble.
Started hungry.
Started holy.

But somewhere between applause and authority…
his heart shifted.
And nobody noticed.
Not at first.
In 2 Chronicles 26, we meet a young king with wind in his lungs and God on his side — Uzziah. Sixteen years old. Crown heavy on his head. Future wide open.
The Scripture says something powerful:
“As long as he sought the Lord, God made him prosper.” (2 Chronicles 26:5)
Read that again.
As long as he sought the Lord…
That’s the open loop.
Because prosperity came.
And it came fast.

He rebuilt cities.
Defeated enemies.
Engineered weapons ahead of his time.
Fortified Jerusalem.
His name spread. His brand exploded. His influence multiplied.
The Bible says his fame spread “far and wide.”

Influencers?
Entrepreneurs?
Leaders building platforms?
Uzziah is your guy.
But then comes the most dangerous verse in the chapter:
“But when he was strong, his heart was lifted up, to his destruction.” (2 Chronicles 26:16)

Strength became self-sufficiency.
Success became self-importance.
Calling became control.
He stepped into the temple to burn incense — a role God reserved only for priests. He crossed a boundary God never gave him permission to cross.
Not because he needed to.
But because he could.
That’s pride.

Not loud arrogance.
Not obvious rebellion.
Just subtle entitlement.

“I built this.”
“I deserve this.”
“I can handle this.”
And in that holy place, in that sacred moment…
leprosy broke out on his forehead.
The very head that had been lifted high.
Public. Visible. Undeniable.
He lived the rest of his days isolated.

Success gave him everything —
except the one thing he needed most:
Humility before God.
Listen to me.
Some scholars interpret Uzziah’s act as a political power move — merging spiritual and royal authority. Others see it simply as spiritual presumption. Either way, the root is clear:
A heart that stopped seeking.
And started assuming.
The tragedy isn’t that he built great things.
The tragedy is that he stopped building his dependence on God.

Entrepreneur.
Content creator.
Leader with momentum.

If growth is increasing your platform but decreasing your prayer life…
you are walking toward the temple with unauthorized fire.
And grace will not compete with pride.
But here’s the Gospel turn.

Uzziah’s story ends in isolation.
But yours doesn’t have to.

Because where Uzziah forced his way into God’s presence…
Jesus tore the veil open for us.
Through Christ alone — not by talent, not by metrics, not by influence — we are invited into the presence of God.
Not to perform.
But to kneel.

At the cross, pride dies.
At the cross, lepers are cleansed.
At the cross, kings bow.

Your success is not your savior.
Jesus is.

Repent of the subtle lift of your heart.
Return to seeking Him daily.
Build the secret altar before you build another tower.
Because the same verse that warns us also guides us:
“As long as he sought the Lord…”
Stay there.
Stay seeking.
And let your influence become incense that honors Christ — not yourself.
We tell the stories that shame tried to erase.
